content.thinking:
For the low-poly camel body, I'll use faceted sweeps with 6-8 sides and smooth shading disabled to get that flat-shaded aesthetic. I need to keep the part count under 1000 and triangles under 60k, so I'll limit the flat color palette to 64 colors to stay efficient.

Now I'm sketching out the oasis scene composition in top-down coordinates—placing the kidney-shaped pond slightly left of center, with a large leaning palm behind-right of it, a second palm leaning from the back-left, and a small young palm plus some bushes nearby. For the tents, I'm positioning a round tent back-left facing toward the pond and a ridge tent to the right facing the opposite way, considering whether to add a small awning attachment without overcrowding the scene.

I'm working out a campfire setup with a ring of stones, a cooking pot, glowing embers, logs, and seating cushions placed near one tent, then figuring out camel placement—a standing adult camel near the palms wearing a saddle blanket, a kneeling camel closer to the first tent, and a small whimsical baby camel next to the standing one, all while refining exact coordinates so nothing overlaps awkwardly.

Now I'm pinning down precise positions and orientations for the third small palm, both tents (one round with an angled doorway, one ridge-style rotated slightly), and the camels—working out yaw angles so each camel faces a sensible direction relative to the pond and camp.

I'll parameterize the camel builder with a stance and scale argument, shrinking the baby's body but enlarging its head proportionally. Then I'm adding a campfire scene with a stone ring, logs, flame shapes, and a pot on a tripod, plus market goods like crates, baskets, and pots near the second tent.

Around the pond I'm scattering reeds using thin spike sweeps with brown cattail heads, flat hexagon lily pads topped with lathe-built lotus flowers, and flat-shaded icosahedron rocks along the edges, along with grass tufts and small flowers. I'm also considering adding a whimsical saguaro cactus on the dunes alongside a skull for desert flavor.

I'm leaning toward skipping extra animals like a fennec fox and keeping things simpler, but I do want a tiny glowing lantern hanging from the tent pole and catenary bunting with extruded triangular flags strung between a palm and the tent for whimsical charm.

For small touches, I'll add flat decal footprints trailing from the camel to the pond, plus a couple of hinge joints for the tent flaps and the swinging lantern, while skipping extras like a windmill or camel head/neck chains to keep the diorama manageable. Now I'm sorting out the ground base thickness and surface height.

For the actual ground plane, I'm keeping the central area flat so objects sit cleanly on top, with dunes only embedded along the back rim and sides so nothing floats awkwardly. Then I'm roughing out camel proportions relative to the tent, settling on a whimsical scale where the camel's hump sits just under tent height even though real camels would dwarf a 3m tent less dramatically.

Now I'm sketching the camel's leg and body construction: four limbs built as tapered sweeps from hip through knee to hoof with pads and toenails, front legs straight and hind legs with a hock bend, plus a body loft defined by cross-section stations running from rump to chest.

For the hump, I'm going with a squashed, low-poly sphere positioned above the back, and considering a draped saddle blanket made from simple trapezoid slabs on each flank rather than a complex extrusion.

I'm leaning toward giving the camel a colorful striped rug draped over the hump rather than tucking it beside it, built as a swept band around the body loop with a rectangular cross-section for thickness.

I could instead try to bake the hump directly into the body loft by shifting the cross-section center upward at certain stations, essentially faking a camel-back profile rather than treating it as a separate mesh that needs a loop seam.

I'm reconsidering the hump shape — maybe keep it as a separate low-poly rounded form overlapping the torso rather than blending into the same cross-section, since a distinct ridge looks cuter. For the blanket, I'm weighing draping a surface over body and hump versus building flat side panels on each flank, leaning toward trying the drape approach on both shapes together.

Separating the hump as its own loop risks messy intersecting contours, so I'll fold it into the body sweep as a single continuous mesh instead — much more robust for draping. I'm shaping the body radius profile so it bumps outward near the hump location, raising both the vertical and horizontal radii slightly to form a tall narrow ridge rather than a separate shape.

I'm sketching the body path as a few catmull-rom points along the spine from rump to chest, then defining how the rx/ry radii taper along that path — narrower at the rump, widest in the middle, slightly tapering toward the chest.

Working through the proportions, I'm checking that the hump height plus body centerline doesn't push the total silhouette too tall, recalculating the top edge from the belly clearance, leg length, and hump bump shift.

To fix the mismatch between camel height and tent height I'm applying a scale factor to shrink the whole camel proportionally, then building a reusable transform function so all local coordinates get scaled and positioned consistently.

Now I'm working out the neck and head geometry: a curved S-shaped sweep from chest to head with tapering radius, then separate upper skull and lower jaw lofts to give the camel a floppy, whimsical muzzle.

For facial details, I'm planning small dark nostril spheres, oversized whimsical eyes with lashes, cone-shaped ears, a forehead hair tuft, and a looping bridle strap around the muzzle.

Next I'm sketching the tail as a thin curved sweep from the rump ending in a brown tuft cluster, then setting up leg placement coordinates for front and hind legs and starting to define the front leg path from shoulder to elbow.

I'm plotting joint curves for front and hind legs with tapering radii for a smooth low-poly look, adding flat cylindrical foot pads resting right at ground level, then working out how to lower and fold the body and legs for a kneeling camel pose, with the front knees touching the ground and lower legs tucked back underneath.

For the baby version, I'm planning to scale the whole body down while making the head proportionally larger for a cuter look.

For the cloth blanket, I'm thinking of it as a membrane stretched between two loop frames positioned around the body's cross-section, including the hump, so it drapes naturally across the camel's back.

For painting it, I'm planning stripe bands running across the membrane's width with gold trim at the edges and a diamond pattern filling the middle section.

For tassels, I'm thinking of adding small downward-pointing spikes along just the bottom edge of the blanket loop, filtering the path points to those low on the y-axis rather than placing them all around.

For the camel's overall structure, I'll transform every point through a unified world-space function so the whole model can be posed and rotated consistently, with surfaces still queried in local model space, and I need to handle how orientation and non-uniform scale interact when placing part geometry like spheres.

For yawed parts, I can use Euler rotation (just a y-axis yaw) alongside non-uniform scale for ellipsoid shapes, saving quaternion or direction-based orientation for actual tilts. I'm sketching a small helper for building scaled, rotated ellipsoids and a general placement class to keep each part positioned and oriented relative to the base group.

Defining placement math...

Now I'm settling on a compact flat color palette for sand and strata layers to keep the asset lightweight.

Still defining the color palette... Now I'm planning the SVG structure: base terrain, dunes, a pond with plants and rocks, then palm trees and other scene elements.

Working out the base outline shape with polar coordinates and noise to give it a hand-drawn, irregular silhouette.

Now I'm planning the extrusion: centering the thickness at a slight offset, adding a small bevel, and considering stacking multiple terraced layers of slightly different scale and height to create a strata-like cliff effect with distinct color bands per layer.

Each layer gets a different scale and vertical phase for irregular, natural-looking edges, with rock colors forming warm earthy strata and a sandy top layer featuring painted ripples where surfaces face upward, while side faces get mottled texture for ruggedness.

I'm working out the texel density needed across the ~20m² of painted surface to keep texture resolution sharp given the 1024² budget.

I think I should bump paintSize to 2048 for finer details like ripples and blanket patterns, accepting the extra atlas weight, and I'm sketching how footprints and dune shapes (using scaled hemisphere geometry sitting on the surface) fit within the base outline.

I'm making sure dunes stay tucked inside the elliptical footprint boundary, normalizing their placement so they don't protrude past the rim, then planning the ripple and shading paint pattern across the dune surface.

Using flat-shaded low-poly hemispheres with light facet segments for the dunes, plus scattered icosahedron pebbles for detail. Now I'm working out the pond shape -- a kidney-like outline defined by a wobbling radius function around an offset center, giving it an organic, uneven border rather than a perfect ellipse.

I'm layering the banks as concentric extruded rings: an outer mottled grass bank, an inner raised rim at a slightly higher elevation to form a lip, and the water surface sitting just below that rim so it reads as contained within a raised edge.

Settling on layered discs: sand band, darker wet-sand edge, then a slightly raised flat water disc for a puddle-like low-poly look, plus rocks and reeds around the rim. For the water surface I'm planning concentric ripple rings based on distance from center, subtle sparkle noise patches, and a lighter shallow-edge band using normalized distance in the paint function.

I'm computing edge-closeness as the ratio of a point's distance from center to the outline's radius at that angle, then using that to blend water colors near the rim. For sparkles I'm adding a handful of tiny flat diamond extrudes scattered on the surface, and for vegetation I'm designing lily pads as circles with a pac-man style wedge cut lying flat on the water, plus a couple lotus flowers made from flattened cone petals arranged on the pads.

Now I'm scattering flattened icosahedron rocks around the pond's edge, adding leaning reed clusters built from tapered sweep geometry with brown capsule-like cattail heads, and generating small grass tufts from clustered cones—planning to merge all these into per-color geometry buckets to keep the part count manageable.

I need to make sure all merged geometries share consistent attributes, so I'm converting indexed shapes like icosahedrons to non-indexed before merging, then applying a flat shading option across the combined mesh.

Budgeting part counts against the 1000 limit, I'm figuring palms, tents, camels, props, and ground will total roughly 500, leaving room to use the bucket approach liberally for tiny repetitive items like grass, pebbles, tassels, and stakes, all attached to the root joint bone.

Now I'm defining the palm tree generator function, building the curved trunk path as a catmull spline through several control points that lean based on offset parameters.

Writing ring stagger logic...

For the crown, I'm placing a brown knob sphere at the top plus a cluster of smaller spheres beneath it to suggest coconuts or hanging dates.

For the fronds, I'm planning 9 of them radiating out with jittered angles, each built from three successive pitched segments (roughly +18°, -10°, -45°) that arch and droop toward the tip, with leaflet outlines tapering narrower as they extend outward.

Still defining leaflet geometry...

Working out the cross product confirms the thickness axis aligns with up, which checks out. For a more natural look I'm considering splitting each frond into two leaflet halves with a slight V-fold, rotating the lateral axis about the direction vector to give them a drooping, folded shape.

Each half becomes its own extruded solid, and with two segments per frond, 7-8 fronds per palm, and two halves per segment, that totals around 28 extrudes per palm, much lighter than the 160-part estimate I was worried about.

For coloring, I'm planning to tint the surface based on position along the frond: faces near the central rib get a lighter shade, while the rest blends from the base frond color toward a darker tone near the tips.

I'll keep rib highlighting thin, add some drooping brown dead fronds and crown knobs for character, and size the big palm at 1.5m with 0.75m fronds versus a smaller 0.9m palm with shorter fronds. Now I'm moving on to designing the round pavilion tent, thinking through a lathe profile that combines a cone roof and cylindrical wall as a solid shape rather than a hollow shell.

For the doorway, I need a dark decal set slightly proud on the wall surface, positioned on one of the octagon's flat faces — I'll need to test the lathe segment spin angle empirically to find where that face centers. I'm also considering an alternative sultan-tent style with a scalloped valance and finial on the roof cone.

I'm sketching the overall tent profile: straight walls up to an overhanging eave lip, then a cone rising to the apex, closing the path back along the axis. For color, I'm thinking of alternating stripe sectors every 45 degrees on the walls in cream and teal, with the roof getting its own pattern.

Now I'm detailing the paint logic further: distinguishing wall from roof by surface normal, giving walls teal/cream stripes and the roof red/cream stripes, plus a gold trim band near the eave based on height. I'm also considering adding a scalloped valance of small triangular extrudes hanging below the eave, alternating red and gold, trying to figure out the right geometry approach for those tangentially-oriented triangles.

Writing triangle geometry helper...

Now I'm planning the door: a dark indigo arched opening cut into the lower wall, extruded slightly outward from the wall surface at a modest width and height.

Then adding gold trim framing it, plus two hinged door flaps rotated open outward via joints pivoting on a vertical axis at the sides.

I'm considering a small interior glimpse into the archway, maybe a lantern, and finishing the apex finial with a swallowtail pennant and gold ball. I'm also adding guy ropes running from the eave down to stakes in the ground at four angles for structural support.

Now I'm planning the front awning canopy with poles and a sloped striped roof slab, plus a doorstep rug with fringe and diamond patterning, cushions as squashed spheres, and a swinging lantern hinged to the awning. Then I'm moving on to the second tent design, starting with an A-frame ridge tent built from a triangular prism outline for a trader stall.

For the roof, I'm using angled box panels forming the two sloped sides, with stripes painted along the downslope direction using local coordinates computed via an inverse transform rather than world space. I also want the tent's front left open with the interior visible, with two tied-back flaps gathered to each side of the entrance.

Adding a ridge pole that extends past the roof peak with finial balls, two slanted front support poles, a hanging banner, and scalloped valance trim along the roof edges, plus crates, a striped sack, and pots near the entrance for camp detail. I'm fixing the ridge tent's proportions to a 0.6 base width, 0.75 length, and 0.5 ridge height, then adding small stitched patch decorations as thin rotated boxes on the roof panels. For the campfire, I'm laying out a ring of eight flat stones with three logs arranged inside.

The fire itself gets layered glowing cone flames in orange and yellow with ember effects, plus whimsical rising smoke puffs made from shrinking icosahedra. I'm adding a cooking pot on a three-rod tripod and a log seat with a cushion nearby for camp furniture.

For market goods, I'm building crates with painted wood-grain and lid-line details, wicker-striped baskets, tied sacks, and lathe-profile amphorae with painted bands and torus handles, along with striped melon spheres, date baskets, and rolled carpets rendered as patterned cylinders.

Near the pond I'm placing a water jug with a hanging bucket, then working out bunting strung between the palm trunk and tent pole — computing catenary rope points and hanging colorful triangular flags along the path, oriented so each flag's plane faces perpendicular to the rope's direction using rotation about the Y axis.

Now I'm turning to the cactus: a stylized saguaro built from swept trunk and arm geometry along curved paths, topped with a pink flower and fine spines.

I'm also sketching a whimsical "OASIS" signpost by the pond edge — a hinged, swinging sign board with text rendered as a texture decal on a front-facing plane, plus considering small extra touches like a half-buried treasure chest with gold coins and footprints in the sand for storytelling detail.

I decide to skip the sleeping traveller idea but add a small bird (sphere body, cone beak, tiny crest) perched on one of the tent poles for charm, keeping camel eyes simple as spheres. With the planning settled, I start writing the actual implementation file, setting up imports for geometry building, path utilities, and framing helpers before laying out the core structure.

Writing a Loc helper class...

Still defining blob helper...

Writing bucket geometry helper...

To be safe I'll clear groups on each geometry before merging to avoid group mismatches. I'm also mapping out how the outline helper converts plan points into extrude coordinates relative to a center position, like for the pond shape.

I'm sketching a slab helper that extrudes a flat plan into a plate of given thickness, and a blob generator that produces wobbly relative outline points for organic shapes.

Now I'm drafting the paint functions for sand ripples using layered noise to create crisp, hard-edged color patches rather than smooth gradients, keeping with the low-poly faceted aesthetic.

For the rock layers, I'm planning stripe and patch paints along the y-axis to simulate sediment strata with distinct colors per band, plus crack patterning. For the top sandy layer, I'm setting up a conditional paint that switches between the ripple pattern on upward-facing surfaces and a dune-sand color on the sides, based on the normal's y-component.

Now I'm moving to the camel's coloring, blending mottled countershading across the coat with lighter tones on the underside, then starting to define the camel builder function itself -- setting up its position, orientation, and a body path curve that dips if the camel is kneeling.

Still writing camel body path...

The bump width at the hump looks right relative to rx. Now I'm setting up the body sweep along the path with octagonal cross-section sides, flat shading, and rounded caps at the chest and rump for smooth dome ends.

Legs get swept polylines too, tapering radius from thigh to ankle with hexagonal flat sides and round caps, plus small flat-shaded knee pad spheres, keeping the coat color consistent throughout.

Adding chest and hoof pads now, darker calluses at the knees for the kneeling pose, flat cylindrical hoof pads colored for hooves, and skipping separate toe details since the body ellipsoid already covers haunch muscle. Next I'm starting the neck as a smooth catmull sweep path beginning inside the chest.

Setting neck control points with tapering radii and flat-sided segments, adjusting for a slight drop and raised head when kneeling, then adding a shaggy mane as small dorsal triangle spikes running along the top of the neck path.

Now I'm defining the head sweep starting from the top of the neck, angled forward and downward about 20 degrees to establish the skull's base position.

For the head itself, I'm lofting a tapered section from the base to the muzzle tip, narrowing width and height as it goes, with faceted six-sided stations for a low-poly look. I'm adding a separate lower jaw loft, lighter in color to suggest droop, plus small dark ellipsoid nostrils near the muzzle end and considering a thin mouth line detail.

Now I'm planning facial expression touches: a curved dark smile sweep along the jaw line, big white eyeballs with dark pupils and tiny eyelash spikes, cone-shaped ears with pink inner cones tilted outward, and little forehead tufts for character. I'm also toying with adding a whimsical tiny buck-tooth and a bridle strap looped around the muzzle as a decorative closed sweep path.

Next I'm sketching out the tail as a tapering sweep from the rump with a tuft of spikes at the end, and considering whether a saddle blanket membrane surface is feasible before falling back to simpler geometry if it proves too tricky.

For the fringe, I'm sampling points along the lower arc of the loop and placing downward-pointing spikes there to form dangling tassels, but I realize the cloth edge is really a full circular cross-section around the belly, so the tassels should hang around both sides rather than just the bottom.

To make it look more like a draped blanket rather than a girth wrap, I'm limiting the geometry to arc slices instead of the full loop -- taking a slice spanning roughly from one side angle to the other, concatenating two sub-arcs since the loop's angle convention runs counter-clockwise about the +Z axis starting from the top.

For the hanging edges, I'm placing tassels along the bottom boundary lines of the cloth where it drapes down each flank, lerping a handful of tassel positions between the two edge endpoints on each side using the loop's parametric points at the cloth's lower bound.

The baby camel gets simplified treatment - smaller scale, no blanket, maybe a bell collar instead of a scarf. For camel A, I'm adding woven basket saddlebags hanging at each side using lathe geometry, with rope connections running up to the top of the blanket, while camel B (kneeling) gets just a saddle plus a bundle sack on its back.

For the kneeling camel's head turn, I want the neck and head to rotate sideways around the neck base point rather than just shifting x-coordinates linearly, so I'm working out a local rotation transform applied to everything above the neck base, parameterized by a turn angle.

I need helper functions for head rotation using direction vectors, plus general body and head position/direction functions, then I'll move into writing the actual frond geometry code.

Writing frond code...

Still working out the sawtooth geometry...

Closing the polygon back to the origin along the rib edge works cleanly without unwanted collinearity. For the full frond, I'm working out the marching logic: each segment gets a pitch angle defining its direction, then I compute left and right side offsets using a perpendicular vector derived from the cross product of direction and tangent, rotated by the leaflet angle.

Verifying that the thickness axis stays properly perpendicular confirms the geometry is sound, with a V-fold angle of 28°. For extrusion I'm setting a thin depth with no bevel, and for coloring I'm deciding to keep it simple with a constant frond color rather than noise-based patching, since the crisp variation felt unnecessary.

For the overall ornament I'm adding drooping dry brown fronds at a lower pitch to give an aged, tilted palm crown look, and I'm working out pitch ranges per frond segment so some fronds curve upward while others droop down, mixing upright newer fronds among older drooping ones. I'm also setting the trunk's lean offset, and now shifting attention to making sure the camel figure doesn't look out of place alongside it.

Now I'm placing the first tent, computing its yaw angle so the doorway orientation faces toward the pond, then setting up a lathed shape for the tent body with striped coloring along its roof and walls using the tent's local orientation frame.

Actually I could compute the stripe angle directly from world position using atan2 on the local coordinates, which works since paint operates on world-space points. For matching stripes to facets, I want the stripe boundaries to line up with the lathe's 8 vertices, so simplest is to just reuse the lathe's own spin parameter for stripe placement rather than reconstructing the angle math myself.

For yaw, I could pick a 45° multiple like yaw 45 to face toward +x+z for variety across tents, avoiding needing exact sign conventions, and keep spin at 22.5+45 offsets to keep the door centered on a facet.

Checking the door width against facet width confirms it fits comfortably within a single facet. Now I'm working out how to index the color stripes by angle so the paint boundaries align with the facet seams rather than crossing them.

Switching to the actual tent geometry, I'm sketching the lathe profile for the body—outline points moving up from the base through the wall height into the lip where the roof cone begins.

I'm figuring out the wall placement: the inward-facing factor from the octagon radius sets where the wall plane sits, and the door gets positioned on the front facet slightly outside that plane with the roof overhang tucked above it so the door height fits cleanly within the wall. Next I want to work out a trim ring around the structure using another lathe sweep.

Working out the eave polygon's vertex angles so the valance triangles align with the local lattice rotation rather than absolute world coordinates.

I'm working out where the hanging triangles attach along the lip edge, figuring they touch the top at the lip radius and hang downward, tangent to each facet's outward direction so they sit flush against the sloped underside.

Now I'm designing the door as an arch shape, defining its outline points to form a rounded Gothic-style top and positioning it on the facet's local coordinate frame with proper width, depth, and orientation.

I'm also adding a gold trim frame around the arch, slightly larger and offset behind it, plus two hinged door flaps that rotate outward 70 degrees from the door's edges to appear open.

Working through the rotation math, I confirm the sign convention: rotating by θ=s*70° about the Y axis makes the flap vector swing outward in +Z, matching the desired open direction regardless of yaw, since Y stays consistent across local and world space.

Now I'm setting up the flap joint and panel geometry — defining the hinge joint, extruding the tapered curtain-shaped outline with appropriate x/y/thickness axes, and planning the tie-back cord and tassel attachments, with posing to be applied after all parts are created.

I'm deciding to skip the awning over the door since the eave lip already provides coverage, and instead sketching the finial for tent 1: a gold-tipped pole rising above the roof with swallowtail pennant flags extruded from a tapered outline.

Now I'm making the pennant a hinge joint attached at the pole top so it can animate with a slight rotation, and planning the four guy ropes running from eave lattice points out to ground stakes at specific angles, skipping the door side.

For the second tent, I'm placing it at (0.9, -0.62) with a yaw around -40° oriented toward the pond, and defining its local proportions: half-width 0.3, ridge height 0.5, and length 0.8 along the z-axis.

Working out the roof panel geometry...

For stripes, I'll paint based on the local z-coordinate of each panel, alternating colors in bands. For the gables, I'll close the back triangle but leave the front open to reveal a dark interior with a rug and cushions inside.

Now I'm adding thin side wall panels under the sloped roof on both sides, sized to match the roof's reach, with striped patterns matching the rest of the tent. The interior stays dark and hollow, visible only through the open front gable against the closed back wall.

I'm also adding a ridge pole extending front and back with gold-capped ends, slanted A-frame support poles at the front gable, and gathered triangular curtain flaps tied back at each side of the entrance opening.

Still defining curtain geometry...

I also need gold finials at the ridge ends, a glowing lantern hanging from the front pole via a hinge joint, plus barrels, cactus, a pond sign, and rocks scattered nearby. Now I'm ready to write the actual code file step by step, starting with a helper function for creating boxes with color, size, position, and optional rotation.

Setting up the root joint and bone structure...

I'm thinking through the base layering: three stacked ring layers for strata and sand with slight scale and phase variation, each extruded with a thin bevel to form the ground terrain.

Now I'm positioning the dunes and camp objects so they stay within a normalized radius on the base ellipse, checking tent footprints against that boundary — tent2's corner extends past the radius, so I need to widen the base ellipse slightly to fit everything.

I shrink the tent dimensions and reposition tent2 to comfortably sit within the base radius, planning to verify the layout visually. For the pond, I'm setting its center and half-axes, and now defining its outline shape function.

Now I'm scaffolding the TypeScript file, importing the builder, math, path, paint, sweep, and texture utilities I'll need, while trimming unused imports to avoid type errors and confirming the Fill type can accept either a string or a Paint object.

I'm defining a Loc helper class that handles local-to-world point transforms, rotation, inverse scaling, and quaternion composition from yaw plus local Euler angles, then starting a small part-building helper function.

I realize all these helpers need access to `b`, so I'll nest them inside the `build()` closure rather than at module level, and I'm setting up a buckets map to group geometries by material/color key.

I'm also planning a geometry cache for shared shapes like icosahedrons and spheres, but I want to be careful about whether `b.part` mutates or clones geometry—if it applies transforms directly to the geometry instance, sharing could cause bugs, so safer to generate fresh geometry via small factory functions each time.

Now I'm sketching helper functions for the base shape: generating a wobbly ring of points for an outline, converting those into a flat 2D plan, and extruding that plan into a flat slab with a given thickness and color.

I'm also parameterizing the slab function to take an optional center offset, so I can use it for the pond's water surface and other centered shapes, plus loops for layered base scales and small footprint outlines before writing the full implementation.

Now I'm writing the palm tree generator, building a curved trunk path with catmull-rom splines and sweeping it with tapering radii.

Adding coconut clusters and hanging dates, then randomizing frond angles with slight jitter...

Now I'm placing three palm trees, working out their positions, lean angles, and heights relative to the pond and tent so they don't overlap too tightly.

I'm shifting tent1's position slightly to avoid crowding, then placing a small campfire and third palm near the camel. I'm sketching out the full layout coordinates for the pond, both tents, and figuring out their yaw angles so the doors face toward the pond.

I'm now adding palm2 and a smaller palm3, then positioning camel A so its yaw orients it facing toward the pond, and starting to work out the baby camel's position and angle nearby.

Next I'm placing a kneeling camel B between the two tents, carefully checking tent footprints and ridge orientations to avoid overlap, settling on a position and a facing angle close to straight ahead.

Then I move to the campfire placement, sizing its base and tripod radius, and start positioning market goods like crates and jars near tent2's front edge. I notice conflicts with a nearby palm tree and camel B, so I shift the palm and try spacing the jars tighter to the tent's left side.

Since the preview tool only gives three-quarter and front views, I'll need to compute positions carefully by hand rather than relying on a top-down check -- I should look at whether preview.ts supports other view angles before resorting to a scratch script.
